narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 59.7% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is above a coin-flip risk, so the review treated you as more likely than not to fail and rejected the application. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty.

The strongest factor increasing that risk was your third-year class standing: your decile was 1.00, while accepted students averaged 5.79. The third most influential factor was your first-year decile, also 1.00 versus an accepted average of 6.00; it again pushed the prediction toward failure. Between them, the second strongest factor was your undergraduate GPA of 3.80, which is higher than the accepted-student average of 3.23. That GPA pushed toward passing and was a protective signal, but it did not outweigh the two class-standing signals.

Next, ask admissions for feedback and whether you can submit updated information. Provide context for your early class standing, show any stronger recent performance, and consider retaking the LSAT if you can improve it, since a stronger score may help. Strengthen your file with legal work, internships, or advanced coursework, and apply to programs that review applicants holistically. Your gender and race were not used in this prediction.
